title: Carpet beetle treatment
subtitle: Filled in 6 Nov 2026 from Australian museum, CSIRO and government sources, not from Mitch. Items marked in orange are for Mitch to confirm.

sections.heading: When this job comes up
body: Customer has carpet beetles. Mitch's service is called Carpet Beetle Treatment. There are very few past jobs, and they were written up as "Call out" and "Call out inspection". [Mitch to confirm: is it an inspection first, then a treatment?]

It is the little hairy grubs (larvae) that eat things, not the adult beetles. They go for dry animal material like wool, fur, feathers and silk, so think rugs, carpet, blankets and stored woollens. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and Museums Victoria, not from Mitch]
The job process, the never list, PPE and the free service period are in the Every job guide. [Mitch to confirm: does the free service period apply to this job?]

sections.heading: How to tell it is carpet beetle
rows: Tiny and rounded, up to about 3 mm, with a mottled pattern of black, orange-brown and white. [Mitch to confirm: from Museums Victoria and Australian Museum, not from Mitch]

Small, brown and hairy, with a brush of hairs at the back end. Bigger than the adult. The hairs break off when handled and can cause an allergic reaction in some people, so keep your gloves on. [Mitch to confirm: from Museums Victoria and Australian Museum, not from Mitch]
Empty, hairy grub skins left behind are a typical sign. [Mitch to confirm: from WA Museum collection care manual, not from Mitch]
Dark droppings (frass) show up best on light-coloured surfaces. [Mitch to confirm: from CSIRO, not from Mitch]
Adult beetles on window sills can mean there is an infestation. The adults fly towards light. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and CSIRO, not from Mitch]
Creamy-white grub in a silk case or under webbing
Not carpet beetle. That is a clothes moth. See the Clothes moth guide. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and WA Museum, not from Mitch]

items.text: Carpet edges, under furniture, along skirting boards and inside wardrobes and closets
items.detail: Grubs hide in dark, undisturbed spots, and adults lay eggs in places like these and in air ducts. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum, not from Mitch]

items.text: Wool, fur, feathers, silk and anything made from animal fibre
items.detail: Rugs, blankets, woollen clothes, stored items. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and WA Museum, not from Mitch]
Dead or live adult beetles. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and CSIRO, not from Mitch]

items.a: Carpet beetles. The beetles are tiny and round. It's the little hairy grubs that do the damage. They eat wool, fur, feathers and silk. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and Museums Victoria, not from Mitch]

The adult beetles live mostly outside and feed on flowers. They fly in, usually towards the light, and lay eggs somewhere dark and quiet like under furniture or skirting boards. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and CSIRO, not from Mitch]

The grubs have fine hairs that break off when handled, and in some people they cause an allergic reaction. Best not to pick them up bare-handed. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum, not from Mitch]

items.q: What can I do to help?
items.a: Vacuum thoroughly and often, especially along carpet edges and under furniture. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum, not from Mitch]

They can. The adults live outside and fly back in easily, so treating inside on its own may not keep them away for good. Regular vacuuming helps. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum, not from Mitch. Check you are happy with this wording]

items.q: Is it safe for the kids and pets?
items.a: Keep kids and pets out of the area while we treat. Follow the product label for when it's safe to come back in. We normally say 1 to 2 hours once it's dry. [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government) and the Every job guide, not from Mitch]

items.q: Can you fix the damage that's already there, or save my rug?
items.a: Our job is the beetles. If it's a precious or badly damaged piece, a textile conservator is the one to ask before anything is done to it. [Mitch to confirm: from Queensland Museum, not from Mitch]
